The example — Unit 1a, done properly end to end

“The first drum” — the 1875 excavation, from archive to screen

The Museum's text names the moment: Museum“Europe wanted to see the grandeur of the past with its own eyes.” We found the real photographs, cited them like a research paper, and built every element from them.

The whole scene in one generation — five shots, twenty seconds, one prompt: the empty dig → the find → the lever → the hands on the fluting → the archaeologist. Cuts landed within a quarter-second of where the script placed them; same characters throughout.

The hero shot — the block settles, the workman turns, the scholar sees. Fifth iteration; every version and its measurements are kept in the working room.

The five units — where each one stands

The Museum's structure is our structure

The Museum’s unit document is the guideline for this whole project. The five units are our research base: we collect information and run tests from each unit for one trailer. We are not producing a film per unit.

MuseumThe five units, as the Museum’s document names them: 1 — From Discovery to Revival · 2 — The First Modern Games & the Olympic Symbols · 3 — The Mesolympic Games, Athens 1906 · 4 — Olympic Values through Sports & Music · 5 — International Olympic Day, a Global Movement.

Wherever you see the Museum mark and italics, the words are the Museum’s own; everything else on this page is our wording.

Unit 1 · From Discovery to Revival (ours: “Revival of the Olympic Games”) scene delivered + key shots

Olympia had been lost to time; the rediscovery reconnects the modern world with ancient Olympic heritage. Then the ancient Games themselves: athletes, musicians, the Sacred Truce, the kotinos as the prize.

1a “The Rediscovery” complete (above); the template for every other scene. The kotinos is this unit’s artefact: “The Crowning” certified hero still + clips and the with/without proof above come from here (this content sat on our old “Victory & honour” card). Wreath-cutting and Oath scenes written with sources and claims ledgers, awaiting production.

Unit 2 · The First Modern Games & the Olympic Symbols (ours: “Symbols & ceremonies”) flagship scene certified

Coubertin and Vikelas, Sorbonne 1894, Athens 1896; then the symbols: the parade, the rings, the flame and torch, motto, flag, anthem, oath.

“The First Flame” (Berlin 1936 torch): finished scene with a formal certificate of provenance; every frame of the animated object is a crop of a verified still. Zero possibility of invention, by construction. The 1896 participation medal is shot (turned over in hands).

Unit 3 · The Mesolympic Games, Athens 1906 cup shots done

Athens 1906: the city modernised, the first national parade, 903 athletes from 21 countries, Sherring’s marathon, cups by sculptors as prizes.

The 1906 Marathon Cup (kantharos form): lifted-overhead clip in two takes plus an anchor still. The 1906 participation medal is digitised and not yet shot; the cheapest win on the board. (Our old “Victory & honour” card stood here; its kotinos content now sits under Unit 1, where the Museum places the wreath.)

Unit 4 · Olympic Values through Sports & Music (ours: “Athletes & their objects”) in progress

Equipment as instruments; rhythm and silence; Excellence, Friendship, Respect. The Museum’s deepest unit: 18 named objects, 17 delivered.

“The Drop” delivered under the person guard; the gymnast composed facing away, because the real team’s identities are not ours to invent. Shoe & racket shots clean on inscriptions. The music thread (equipment as instruments, rhythm) is not yet shot.

Unit 5 · International Olympic Day, a Global Movement (ours: “Legacy”) not started · digital-content unit

Olympic Day, 23 June: the IOC’s founding date, the Olympic Day Run in 150+ countries, the Museum in Thessaloniki as organiser.

No physical artefacts in this unit; the Museum plans digital video content here. Nothing produced yet. The kotinos shown stands for the thread from the ancient prize to today.

The safeguards — what makes this different from every AI video

Rules that were earned, not written

  • Inscriptions live in the ledger, not the pixels. Tests showed generated text comes out legible and wrong (8.41 became 8.71). So engraved surfaces are turned away or cropped, and what they say is documented instead.
  • Every claim is typed. Each shot states what it asserts — Sourced, Assumed (with confidence), or Invented — and what it deliberately does not show. Where the record is silent, we say so.
  • Quality is measured, not felt. Scale ratios, colour agreement, cut timing — numbers in a ledger per candidate, because a rule in the prompt reduces errors but never eliminates them.
  • Everything is versioned. Five iterations of the hero shot exist with their measurements; nothing is quietly replaced. The industry’s own training material contains no accuracy discipline at all — this layer is ours.

The campaign — emotion and proof in one cut

The Hands Remember

Thirty seconds, four real objects from the collection: Tentoglou's shoes, the 1976 belt, the Sydney clubs, the kotinos. The emotion is generated; the handwriting is not — the two ink close-ups are computed camera moves over the Museum's own digitisations, so the athlete's real ink is on screen because it is true. The AI take that forged the same ink is preserved and published beside the final cut (#103 in the working room) — the difference between the two is exactly what this project exists to guarantee.

The system behind it

What is Empirica?

Empirica is a system for measured AI work. Every AI practitioner in this pipeline works inside it: before acting it states what it knows and what it merely assumes; every claim is logged with its source; every mistake stays on record. The claim ledgers, the safeguards and the versioned measurements on this page are Empirica working as designed. It is how a generative pipeline can be held to museum standards.

Empirica is a startup financed by FFP, currently in testing. It was not built for this project; that it does what the REEVALUATE enablers set out to enable is a happy coincidence. The core is open source. A proprietary paid layer, Cortex (monthly subscription), lets the different AI practices communicate and coordinate with each other.

What you see on this site is a complete generative-AI pipeline built on Empirica: brief, storyboard, image, video, review, with provenance enforced at every step. Because the whole chain is measured and logged, this work can also serve as an open case study for the public.

Next steps

The method is proven on one scene. Next: one trailer, drawing on all five units.

  1. Collect from each unit what the trailer needs: key moments, artefacts, references (as done for 1a), and test them with the same pipeline (research → sheets → start frame → one generation → review). Tests per unit, not a film per unit.
  2. Finish Units 3–4 (remaining Crowning and athlete-object shots — specs ready).
  3. Two decisions pending: replenish video-generation credits, and whether to trial 3D scene-blocking — placing the Museum's own 3D meshes in the virtual set, so the digitised geometry itself controls the frame.
